**Important Note**
Each R code chunk runs as its own separate entity so no chunk needs to have a previous chunk run before it to work. This is because they all draw data from the same /Data folder in the Zip drive as their starting active dataset. Since this is all large data manipulation down towards smaller more manageable datasets, only run that code where you want to see what the output creates. Whenever possible, tables that result from the output generated are shown.

# Initial Generation of the Virginia Dataset.

## How to correctly download the initial data.

To correctly generate the initial dataset to use in the follow up charts and graphs follow these directions.

1. Navigate to this website: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/sobhanmoosavi/us-accidents?resource=download
2. Click download in the upper right hand corner of the website.
3. Click download dataset as zip.
4. Click the file that opens.
5. Click extract all.
6. Extract it to the local folder labeled Data so that the code can work.


## Validation Code and Extraction of Virginia from the full dataset. 

The below code extracts from the full dataset file those rows that have the value under "State" = VA. This is in an effort to try to get a Virginia dataset only to draw graphs and run code on.

**The two errors to gaurd against here are:** 1. in the underlying dataset, the authors can always choose to add additional columns to the Dataset to explore different effects on traffic. If you do not run the set up code and just use the Virginia dataset only without checks, you might miss the inclusion of these additional columns when the code is run. 2. the authors of the dataset can always choose to be inconsistent and abbreviate Virginia as VA, va, or type the full name of Virginia out. Since our analysis is based on Virginia data only, we want to make sure when we pull Virginia out of the full dataset that we are getting all Virginia records, and not just the part with only the abbreviation VA. We also want to make sure we are getting all columns to start building the dataset. This validation code checks for both parts by setting up the test and then setting up a falsification procedure as well (i.e. if the test passes everything, how do we know our test even does the correct job). Then to perform effective memory handling, at the end it kills the corrupt dataframes in the R image that were used in the falsification procedure, and the full data set once the Virginia dataset has been written to /Data.This leaves only dfva in the image space as a Virginia only dataset.

Note, please turn eval = true to run the full code to see what it does.

```{r create_VA_dataset}
#| eval: true

# ==========================================================================
# STEP 1: FAST FILTER TO VIRGINIA & SAVE SUBSET
# ==========================================================================

#Bring Full table in
dffull<- fread("../Data/US_Accidents_March23.csv")%>%
  as_tibble()

# Filter full table as just state
dfva <- dffull |>
  filter(State == "VA")

# Verify that the data brought in has the same dimensions as the full dataset
# Verify dfva is the same column dimensions as the full
check_col <- function(x, y){
  stopifnot(ncol(x) == ncol(y))   
  invisible(TRUE)
}

#create corruption (AI)
set.seed(123)
dfvacor<-dfva |> 
  mutate(corcol = rnorm(nrow(dfva), mean = 50, sd = 10))

#Verify works on original and fails on corrupted.
c(passes_originalnew = !inherits(try(check_col(dffull, dfva), silent = TRUE), "try-error"),
  rejects_corruptnew =  inherits(try(check_col(dffull, dfvacor), silent = TRUE), "try-error"))

#---------------------
### --- Verify ALL Virginia observations were pulled in (Completeness & Alias Check) AI generated
check_va_complete <- function(x, y) {
  # 1. Count exact "VA" matches in the full dataset
  expected_n <- sum(x$State == "VA", na.rm = TRUE)
  # 2. Standardize strings (uppercase, trim whitespace, remove periods)
  clean_state <- gsub("\\.", "", trimws(toupper(x$State)))
  # 3. Count all possible Virginia representations ("VA", "VIRGINIA", "VA.", etc.)
  clean_n <- sum(clean_state %in% c("VA", "VIRGINIA"), na.rm = TRUE)
  stopifnot(
    !anyNA(y$State),
    all(y$State == "VA"),
    nrow(y) == expected_n,
    expected_n == clean_n
  )
  invisible(TRUE)
}

# Create corruption 1: Simulate dropping 10 rows from dfva
dfva_incomplete <- dfva |> 
  slice(-c(1:10))

# Create corruption 2: Simulate someone typing "Virginia" instead of "VA" in dffull
dffull_bad_spelling <- dffull
dffull_bad_spelling$State[which(dffull$State == "VA")[1]] <- "Virginia"

# Verify works on original and fails on both corruptions
c(passes_original        = !inherits(try(check_va_complete(dffull, dfva), silent = TRUE), "try-error"),
  rejects_dropped_rows   =  inherits(try(check_va_complete(dffull, dfva_incomplete), silent = TRUE), "try-error"),
  rejects_virginia_spell =  inherits(try(check_va_complete(dffull_bad_spelling, y), silent = TRUE), "try-error"))
# Write VA Only Dataset------------------------------

write_csv(dfva, "../Data/Virginia_Accidents.csv")
gc()
#Remove Unneeded memory from R Global Environment.----------------------
rm(dfvacor,dffull, dffull_bad_spelling, dfva_incomplete)
```

## Attempting Join of the Virginia Dataset with the US Census Bureau data.

This code realizes that the Virginia Dataset by itself will unfairly bias results to the more populous counties as the "most accidents" are likely to occur in the biggest counties by virtue of the fact that there are just simply more people on the road. So we thought it might be helpful to try to link the current dataset using a join to a Census Bureau population dataset for Virginia counties.We can then weight our count of accidents by the population in each county to show a rate instead of a raw count of accidents per county.

Our dataset from kaggle offers two possibilities to join to a population data set. First, our dataset has "Counties" as a column variable. It should be possible, but complicated, to do text editing and link this column to the Census data.  Second, our dataset has geolocation data such as longitude and latitude of the accident. Because analyzing counties was important to us with our question, we choose the first method as it seemed to have a stronger tie to the original county column in the dataset and the exact geo-location of the accident may not be a 1-1 tie to the official US Census Bureau county name given in our Kaggle dataset.Then we used the geolocation dataset as a verification check with the idea that if there is a low disagreement between what the geolocated data of the accident would say regarding the location of the accident, and the county name, then we can trust the population values we are drawing from the Census Bureau. The verification check also made sure using anti_join, that we were not missing any Virginia populations. 

Finally, at the end, un-needed dataframes were removed from the R image for efficient memory storage.

Switch eval = false to true to see what the code does.

```{r join_with_US_Census_Bureau}
#| eval: true
# ==========================================================================
# FETCH & CLEAN OFFICIAL US CENSUS POPULATION DATA FOR VIRGINIA
# ==========================================================================

dfva<-read.csv("../Data/Virginia_Accidents.csv")

census_url <- "https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2023/counties/totals/co-est2023-alldata.csv"

va_pop <- read_csv(
  census_url,
  locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  filter(STNAME == "Virginia", SUMLEV == "050") %>% # 050 = All 133 VA Counties & Independent Cities
  transmute(
    GEOID       = paste0(STATE, COUNTY),
    census_name = str_squish(CTYNAME),
    census_key  = str_to_lower(census_name),
    population  = POPESTIMATE2023
  )

# ==========================================================================
#  HARMONIZE VIRGINIA COUNTY & INDEPENDENT CITY NAMES
# ==========================================================================
# The 34 VA independent cities that do NOT share a name with a surrounding county
unambiguous_va_cities <- c(
  "alexandria", "bristol", "buena vista", "charlottesville", "chesapeake",
  "colonial heights", "covington", "danville", "emporia", "falls church",
  "fredericksburg", "galax", "hampton", "harrisonburg", "hopewell",
  "lexington", "lynchburg", "manassas", "manassas park", "martinsville",
  "newport news", "norfolk", "norton", "petersburg", "poquoson",
  "portsmouth", "radford", "salem", "staunton", "suffolk",
  "virginia beach", "waynesboro", "williamsburg", "winchester"
)

dfva_clean <- dfva %>%
  mutate(
    # 1. Standardize encoding, remove parentheses around "(city)" or "(county)", and lowercase
    cnty_raw   = str_to_lower(str_squish(iconv(County, to = "UTF-8", sub = ""))),
    cnty_clean = str_squish(str_replace_all(cnty_raw, "[()]", "")),
    
    # 2. Extract base name by stripping trailing " county" or " city"
    cnty_base  = str_remove(cnty_clean, "\\s+(county|city)$"),
    
    # 3. Map every jurisdiction 1-to-1 from the County column to the Census CTYNAME format
    census_key = case_when(
      # Fix the 2 Virginia counties that literally have "City" in their county name
      cnty_base %in% c("james", "james city") ~ "james city county",
      cnty_base %in% c("charles", "charles city") ~ "charles city county",
      
      # Bedford city merged into Bedford County in 2013
      cnty_base == "bedford" ~ "bedford county",
      
      # Resolve the 4 VA County vs. Independent City collisions (Fairfax, Roanoke, Richmond, Franklin)
      # Because raw independent cities are labeled "(city)" or "city", keep them as "city", 
      # and map plain "Fairfax" / "Roanoke" / "Richmond" / "Franklin" directly to "county"
      cnty_clean %in% c("fairfax city", "roanoke city", "richmond city", "franklin city") ~ cnty_clean,
      str_detect(cnty_clean, "^city of (fairfax|roanoke|richmond|franklin)$") ~ paste0(str_remove(cnty_clean, "^city of "), " city"),
      cnty_base %in% c("fairfax", "roanoke", "richmond", "franklin") ~ paste0(cnty_base, " county"),
      
      # Append " city" to the 34 unambiguous independent cities
      cnty_base %in% unambiguous_va_cities ~ paste0(cnty_base, " city"),
      
      # Append " county" to all remaining Virginia counties
      !is.na(cnty_base) & cnty_base != "" ~ paste0(cnty_base, " county"),
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )



#---------------------------------

# Verify 100% match rate against Census
unmatched <- dfva_clean %>%
  anti_join(va_pop, by = "census_key") %>%
  count(County, City, census_key, sort = TRUE)

print(unmatched)

# 2. Left join population data onto the accident records and remove helper columns
dfva_joined <- dfva_clean %>%
  left_join(va_pop, by = "census_key") %>%
  select(-cnty_raw, -cnty_clean, -cnty_base)

# ==========================================================================
# STEP 5 SPATIAL AUDIT COMPARING COUNTY TEXT VS. GPS COORDINATES
# ==========================================================================


# cb = FALSE uses full legal boundaries (including bridges over water in Hampton Roads/Arlington)
va_polygons <- counties(state = "VA", cb = FALSE, year = 2022) %>%
  transmute(
    spatial_GEOID = GEOID,
    spatial_name  = NAMELSAD,
    spatial_key   = str_to_lower(str_squish(NAMELSAD))
  )

dfva_audit <- dfva_clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(Start_Lng), !is.na(Start_Lat)) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Start_Lng", "Start_Lat"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(va_polygons)) %>%
  st_join(va_polygons, join = st_within) %>%
  st_drop_geometry()

audit_summary <- dfva_audit %>%
  summarise(
    total_rows       = n(),
    exact_matches    = sum(census_key == spatial_key, na.rm = TRUE),
    mismatches       = sum(census_key != spatial_key, na.rm = TRUE),
    outside_va_poly  = sum(is.na(spatial_key)),
    match_percentage = round((exact_matches / total_rows) * 100, 2)
  )

print(audit_summary)

mismatch_breakdown <- dfva_audit %>%
  filter(census_key != spatial_key | is.na(spatial_key)) %>%
  count(County, City, text_assigned = census_key, gps_assigned = spatial_key, sort = TRUE)

# Summary Table Formulations -----
dfva_county_summary <- dfva_joined %>%
  group_by(GEOID, census_name, population) %>%
  summarise(
    total_accidents  = n(),
    severe_accidents = sum(Severity >= 3, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_severity     = mean(Severity, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    accidents_per_person = total_accidents / population,
    accidents_per_100k   = (total_accidents / population) * 100000,
    severe_per_100k      = (severe_accidents / population) * 100000
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(accidents_per_100k))

##Remove Unneeded Memory from R image-------------------------------------
rm(dfva, dfva_clean, dfva_audit)

## Write the joined dataset
# Save full row-level Virginia dataset with Census population attached
write_csv(dfva_joined, "../Data/Virginia_Accidents_With_Pop.csv")
```

```{r graphs_and_charts}
###---------------------- Graphing
dfva_joined <- read.csv("../Data/Virginia_Accidents_With_Pop.csv")

acc<-dfva_joined

summary(acc)

table(acc$Severity)
summary(acc$`Precipitation(in)`)


acc <- acc %>% mutate(severe = Severity >= 3)

acc %>%
  filter(!is.na(Severity)) %>%
  count(Severity) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Severity), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Virginia Car Accidents by Severity",
    x = "Accident Severity",
    y = "Number of Accidents")


acc %>%
  summarise(
    total_accidents = n(),
    severe_accidents = sum(severe, na.rm = TRUE),
    severe_percent = mean(severe, na.rm = TRUE) * 100
  )

acc %>%
  filter(!is.na(Weather_Condition)) %>%
  count(Weather_Condition, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 12) %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(x = reorder(Weather_Condition, n), y = n)
  ) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Most Common Weather Conditions During Accidents",
    x = "Weather Condition",
    y = "Number of Accidents"
  )

weather_summary <- acc %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(Weather_Condition),
    !is.na(Severity)
  ) %>%
  group_by(Weather_Condition) %>%
  summarise(
    accidents = n(),
    severe_percent = mean(Severity >= 3) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(accidents >= 100) %>%
  arrange(desc(severe_percent))

weather_summary %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = reorder(Weather_Condition, severe_percent),
      y = severe_percent
    )
  ) +
  geom_col(fill = "firebrick") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Percentage of Severe Accidents by Weather",
    subtitle = "Conditions with at least 100 recorded accidents",
    x = "Weather Condition",
    y = "Severe Accidents (%)"
  )

road_features <- c(
  "Junction",
  "Crossing",
  "Traffic_Signal",
  "Stop",
  "Railway",
  "Traffic_Calming",
  "Roundabout",
  "Give_Way",
  "Amenity",
  "Bump",
  "No_Exit",
  "Turning_Loop",
  "Station"
)

road_summary <- acc %>%
  select(Severity, all_of(road_features)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(road_features),
    names_to = "road_feature",
    values_to = "present"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(present), !is.na(Severity)) %>%
  group_by(road_feature, present) %>%
  summarise(
    accidents = n(),
    severe_percent = mean(Severity >= 3) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  road_summary,
  aes(
    x = road_feature,
    y = severe_percent,
    fill = factor(present)
  )
) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Accident Severity by Road Feature",
    x = "Road Feature",
    y = "Severe Accidents (%)",
    fill = "Feature Present"
  )



county_summary <- acc %>%
  filter(!is.na(County)) %>%
  group_by(County) %>%
  summarise(
    accidents = n(),
    severe_accidents = sum(severe, na.rm = TRUE),
    severe_percent = mean(severe, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(accidents))

county_summary %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(x = reorder(County, accidents), y = accidents)
  ) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkslateblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Virginia Counties with the Most Recorded Accidents",
    x = "County",
    y = "Number of Accidents"
  ) 
```
